body:
Two connected struggles for India's freedom

Between 1914 and 1947, the Indian National Movement developed through constitutional negotiations, political protests and events that changed public opinion. British authorities introduced limited reforms and appointed commissions, while Indian leaders demanded a greater share in government and eventually complete independence.

The important developments of this period must be understood as different kinds of events. A commission investigated a problem and made recommendations. A constitutional report proposed a future system of government. A conference or mission attempted to secure political agreement. An Act passed by the British Parliament could create a legal framework for administration. Episodes such as the Komagata Maru incident, the Indian National Army trials and the Noakhali violence affected the freedom struggle without themselves being constitutional reforms.

The main developments and their purposes

  • 1914 — Komagata Maru: The exclusion of Indian passengers from Canada demonstrated racial discrimination within the British Empire.
  • 1919 — Government of India Act: The British introduced dyarchy in the provinces, dividing administrative subjects into reserved and transferred categories.
  • 1927–1928 — Simon Commission: An all-British commission appointed to review constitutional arrangements faced widespread Indian opposition.
  • 1928 — Nehru Report: Indian leaders produced a constitutional proposal demanding dominion status and responsible government.
  • 1930–1932 — Round Table Conferences: Three conferences in London discussed India's future constitutional structure.
  • 1935 — Government of India Act: A new constitutional law provided for provincial autonomy and proposed an all-India federation.
  • 1942 — Cripps Mission: Britain offered a post-war constitutional settlement but did not transfer immediate control of defence.
  • 1945–1946 — INA trials: The prosecution of Indian National Army officers produced widespread nationalist sympathy.
  • 1946 — Cabinet Mission: A British mission proposed a united Indian constitutional arrangement and a Constituent Assembly.
  • 1946–1947 — Noakhali: Communal violence in eastern Bengal led Mahatma Gandhi to undertake a peace mission.

Why constitutional status matters

A proposal and an enacted law are not the same. The Nehru Report of 1928 expressed a proposed Indian constitutional arrangement, but it did not become the constitution of British India. The Government of India Act of 1935, by contrast, was an enacted law, although not every provision was brought into operation.

The same distinction applies to the British missions. The Cripps proposals of 1942 were not accepted as a settlement. The Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 helped establish the process for forming a Constituent Assembly, but its proposed united constitutional structure did not become the final arrangement under which India attained independence.

Prelims focus

  • 1919 and 1935 are the years of 2 important Government of India Acts.
  • The Simon Commission was appointed in 1927 and arrived in India in 1928.
  • The Nehru Report was prepared in 1928.
  • The Round Table Conferences took place during 1930–1932.
  • The Cripps Mission came in 1942; the Cabinet Mission came in 1946.
  • Trap: A commission's recommendation or a mission's proposal should not be treated as an enacted constitutional provision.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 120–126; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, Chapter 2, Nationalism in India, printed pp. 62–65; UK House of Lords Library, Lord Sinha of Raipur and the Government of India Act 1919, 13 December 2019, pp. 2–4; UK Parliament, Cabinet Mission Statement, House of Lords Debates, 16 May 1946, consulted 22 November 2026.]

title: Understanding the Constitutional and Political Developments of 1914–1947

body:
Background: Indians as British subjects

Before independence, Indians were subjects of the British Empire. However, this common imperial status did not guarantee equal rights to enter or settle in every British territory. Canada, which was part of the British Empire, maintained immigration restrictions that discriminated against people arriving from Asia.

One important restriction was Canada's Continuous Journey regulation. It required immigrants to travel directly from their country of origin to Canada without interrupting the journey. At that time, there was no regular direct steamship service from India to Canada. The rule therefore created a major practical obstacle for prospective Indian immigrants.

Continuous Journey regulation

A Canadian immigration restriction requiring an uninterrupted journey from the country of origin. Its practical effect was to obstruct immigration from India.

The voyage of the Komagata Maru

In 1914, Gurdit Singh, a Sikh businessman, chartered a Japanese steamship known as the Komagata Maru. It was also renamed Guru Nanak Jahaz. The voyage was intended to challenge discriminatory immigration restrictions and enable Indian passengers to enter Canada.

The ship departed from Hong Kong on 4 April 1914 and travelled through East Asian ports towards Canada. It carried 376 passengers, most of whom came from Punjab. The commonly recorded composition was approximately 340 Sikhs, 24 Muslims and 12 Hindus.

On 23 May 1914, the ship reached Vancouver, on Canada's Pacific coast. Canadian authorities refused entry to most passengers, arguing that the requirements of the Continuous Journey regulation had not been satisfied. Approximately 20 passengers who had previously lived in Canada were permitted to disembark; the remaining passengers were prevented from entering.

Forced departure and the Budge Budge confrontation

The passengers remained aboard the ship for about 2 months while the dispute continued. On 23 July 1914, Canadian authorities forced the vessel to leave Vancouver.

After the ship returned to British India, a confrontation occurred at Budge Budge, near Calcutta, on 29 September 1914. British Indian police and troops confronted the passengers, and 19 passengers were killed. Many others faced detention or restrictions.

Significance for the Indian National Movement

The incident exposed the contradiction between Indians' position as British subjects and the unequal treatment they faced elsewhere in the Empire. It intensified criticism of imperial racial discrimination and became associated with the growing political awareness of overseas Indians.

The episode also helps distinguish overseas discrimination from repression within British India. Vancouver was the location where most passengers were denied entry. Budge Budge was the location of the later confrontation after the ship's return.

The Komagata Maru was a passenger ship, not a British constitutional commission or an Indian political organisation. Its significance lies in the discrimination faced by its passengers and the subsequent confrontation in India.

Prelims focus

  • Year: 1914.
  • Person associated with chartering the ship: Gurdit Singh.
  • Number of passengers: 376.
  • Vancouver arrival: 23 May 1914; forced departure: 23 July 1914.
  • Budge Budge confrontation: 29 September 1914; 19 passengers were killed.
  • Trap: Vancouver was in Canada; Budge Budge was near Calcutta in British India.

[City of Vancouver, Guru Nanak Jahaz (Komagata Maru) Place, sections History, The Passengers, Denied Entry in Vancouver, Continuous Journey Regulation and Tragic Outcome in India, consulted 22 November 2026; Parks Canada, Komagata Maru National Historic Event, historical background, consulted 22 November 2026.]

title: Komagata Maru Incident, 1914: Immigration Discrimination and Nationalist Reaction

body:
Government of India Act, 1919

The Government of India Act, 1919 followed the Montagu–Chelmsford reforms. Edwin Montagu was the British Secretary of State for India, and Lord Chelmsford was the Viceroy. Their proposals aimed to expand Indian participation in government gradually, without immediately establishing full responsible government.

The Act introduced dyarchy in the provinces. Dyarchy means a system in which administrative responsibility is divided between 2 authorities. Provincial subjects were separated into reserved and transferred subjects.

Reserved subjects

Reserved subjects remained under the control of the provincial Governor and his executive councillors. Examples included police, law and order, land revenue and major financial administration. Ministers responsible to the elected provincial legislature did not control these matters.

Transferred subjects

Transferred subjects were administered by Indian ministers who were responsible to the provincial legislative council. Examples included education, public health, agriculture and local self-government. This arrangement gave Indians experience in administering selected departments, but their authority remained limited by the wider powers of the Governor.

1919 dyarchy operated at the provincial level. It was not a division of the central government into reserved and transferred departments.

Changes at the centre

The Act also established a bicameral central legislature, consisting of the Council of State and the Legislative Assembly. Bicameral means having 2 legislative chambers. Voting rights remained restricted, and the Governor-General retained extensive executive powers. The central executive did not become responsible to an Indian parliamentary majority.

The Act provided for a later statutory examination of constitutional progress. This review requirement led to the appointment of the Simon Commission in 1927.

Government of India Act, 1935

After further political demands, investigations and constitutional discussions, the British Parliament enacted the Government of India Act, 1935. It was a major revision of the colonial constitutional system, but it did not grant India independence.

Provincial autonomy

The Act abolished provincial dyarchy and provided for provincial autonomy. In the new arrangement, provincial ministers could administer a wider range of provincial subjects and were generally responsible to elected legislatures. Nevertheless, provincial Governors retained special responsibilities and discretionary powers. Autonomy therefore did not mean complete freedom from British control.

Provincial elections were held in 1937, after which ministries were formed under the new arrangements.

Proposed federation and central dyarchy

The Act proposed an all-India federation consisting of British Indian provinces and princely states. A federation is a constitutional system in which powers are divided between a central authority and constituent units. The proposed federation depended on the participation of princely states and never came into operation.

The Act also provided for dyarchy at the federal centre, but this provision was tied to the unimplemented federal scheme. It is therefore incorrect to say that central dyarchy actually operated under the 1935 Act.

The Act divided legislative subjects into Federal, Provincial and Concurrent Lists. Concurrent subjects were matters on which both the proposed federal legislature and provincial legislatures could make laws, with federal law normally prevailing in a conflict. A provincial law reserved for and receiving the Governor-General's or Crown's assent could prevail over earlier conflicting law in that province, subject to subsequent federal legislation.

Comparison of the 2 Acts

FeatureAct of 1919Act of 1935
Provincial administrationIntroduced dyarchyAbolished dyarchy and provided autonomy
Provincial ministersControlled transferred subjects onlyAdministered a wider range of provincial subjects
Central arrangementBicameral legislature; no central dyarchyProposed federation and central dyarchy
ImplementationProvincial dyarchy operatedProvincial autonomy operated; proposed federation did not

Why the distinction matters

The 1919 and 1935 Acts are often linked to constitutional progress, but their effects were different. The 1919 Act introduced provincial dyarchy; the 1935 Act ended it. The 1935 Act is associated with provincial autonomy, while its proposed federal structure remained unimplemented.

Prelims focus

  • The Montagu–Chelmsford reforms formed the basis of the 1919 Act.
  • Under the 1919 Act, education and public health were transferred subjects.
  • Under the 1919 Act, police and land revenue were reserved subjects.
  • The 1935 Act abolished provincial dyarchy.
  • Provincial autonomy operated after the 1937 elections.
  • Trap: The 1935 Act proposed central dyarchy and an all-India federation; neither operated as originally envisaged.

[UK House of Lords Library, Lord Sinha of Raipur and the Government of India Act 1919, 13 December 2019, pp. 2–4; Government of India Act, 1935, provisions on provincial government and federation; NCERT, Indian Constitution at Work, Class 11, Chapter 1, Constitution: Why and How?, printed pp. 14–16; consulted 22 November 2026.]
